# Exit interviews, conducted by voice and coded at scale

Most analytics use cases for voice are bad. Voice is a poor way to deliver a
number — you can't hold six figures in your head from audio, you can't look at
it twice, and any answer needing a table needs a screen.

But that's voice as *output*. This is voice as **input**, which is the
direction where it actually wins: people say more out loud than they type, they
elaborate when prompted, and they'll tell an agent things they won't put in a
form their manager might read.

**All data here is synthetic.** 120 interviews generated by
`scripts/seed_interviews.py`. No real person's exit interview is represented.

---

## The problem

Exit interviews are done badly for structural reasons. Line managers conduct
them, so nobody says the true thing when the manager *is* the thing. HR
conducts them, which is honest but covers a fraction of leavers. Or it's a
form, which scales perfectly and collects nothing — a form can't ask "what do
you mean by that?"

So most organisations have low coverage, inconsistent questioning, and a pile
of free text nobody codes. Turnover reporting ends up as a number with no
attached reason, which means it can be discussed but not acted on.

---

## What this does

```
Voice ──▶ ElevenLabs agent ──▶ post-call webhook ──▶ Groq coding ──▶ SQLite
                                                                       │
                                                           aggregate ◀──┘
                                                           dashboard
```

An agent conducts a structured eight-question interview with probing. The
transcript is coded against a fixed frame, every interview, automatically. The
dashboard shows the aggregate.

Automated coding is the part that matters. Manual coding is why organisations
code a sample rather than the population; removing that constraint is what
makes 100% coverage possible.

---

## The coding frame

Full definitions in [`app/schema.py`](app/schema.py). Two fields do most of the
work:

**`preventability`** — could the organisation realistically have kept this
person? Exit reporting that doesn't separate preventable from unpreventable
produces a number nobody can act on, because "relocating to Scotland" and "my
supervisor was difficult" land in the same bucket.

**`intent_timing`** — how long before resigning did they first start thinking
about it? This is the most useful question in exit interviewing and it's almost
never asked. It sizes your intervention window. If people decide at month one
and leave at month six, you had five months of warning.

Also coded: primary and secondary drivers, trigger type, sentiment, manager
sentiment, would-return, free themes, and one verbatim.

---

## What the sample shows

- ~80% of leaving coded preventable or partially preventable
- ~31% first thought about leaving within three months of joining
- Preventable leaving concentrated at Northgate nights, driven by commute
- Recurring themes there: *"night bus stopped running"*, *"shift pattern not
  explained at interview"*

The last one matters most. It says the problem starts at hiring, not at week
six — people are being recruited into a shift they can't physically get home
from, and nobody mentions it until they're in the car park at 6am.

**This triangulates with the quantitative data.** Attrition figures flag
Northgate nights on volume; exit interviews say why. Two independent signals
pointing the same way is a finding. One on its own is a hypothesis.

---

## Methodology notes

Two things here were wrong in the first build and are worth understanding,
because they're the kind of error that survives into production quietly.

**Minimum segment size.** With a threshold of four interviews, a segment with
four preventable codes reports 100% and tops the ranking on noise alone. The
first version did exactly this and surfaced the wrong site. Segments below
threshold are now returned separately, flagged and unranked — reported, not
silently dropped.

**Ranking on volume before rate.** A segment losing 24 people preventably
matters more than one losing 6, even at a lower percentage. Sorting on
percentage alone puts small, noisy segments at the top of a list that people
will read as a priority order.

## Running locally

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
python scripts/seed_interviews.py
uvicorn app.main:app --reload
```

Dashboard at `http://localhost:8000`, API under `/api/`.

Live interviews need `GROQ_API_KEY`. The seeded ones are pre-coded, so the
dashboard works without it.

---

## Deploying

Render free tier, blueprint included:

```bash
git init && git add . && git commit -m "Initial build"
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/exit-interviews.git
git push -u origin main
```

Then **render.com → New → Blueprint**. Set `GROQ_API_KEY`,
`ELEVENLABS_WEBHOOK_SECRET` and `ELEVENLABS_AGENT_ID`.

Commit `data/interviews.db` — Render's free filesystem is ephemeral, so
shipping the seeded database is what makes the dashboard work on a cold deploy.
Live interviews are lost on redeploy. For anything real, use a mounted disk or
managed Postgres.

---

## Ethics

Handling sensitive disclosures from people at a vulnerable moment. See
[`AGENT_SETUP.md`](AGENT_SETUP.md) for the full handling. In short: explicit
consent before the first question, discard on refusal rather than store-and-
filter, aggregate reporting with a minimum segment size, a human route always
available, defined retention, and a hard stop that routes to a named person if
anyone discloses bullying, harassment or discrimination.

That last one is the most important line in the prompt. An agent that treats a
harassment disclosure as another data point is worse than no agent.

---

## What I'd conclude

It works, and it's still the wrong instrument.

Exit interviews are the worst possible moment to collect this. People are
demob-happy, or angry, or being careful to protect a reference. And by
definition you're asking after the outcome you wanted to prevent.

The data makes its own argument: if a third of leavers decide within three
months, the right instrument is a **stay interview at week six**, not an exit
interview at month nine. Same agent, same coding frame, same pipeline —
different moment, and one where the answer can still change something.

So the honest framing of this project is that it's a well-built version of the
wrong thing, which turned out to be the fastest way to work out what the right
thing was.

---
